proofs.proof_tex:
For \(k\in\{2,4,6\}\), let \(\pi_k\) denote the certificate prior and, for every full-count cell with positive predictive mass, write
\[
 A_{xy}^{(k)}=\sum_{N\in\mathcal N_k}\pi_{k,N}K_N(x,y),
 \qquad
 B_{xy}^{(k)}=\sum_{N\in\mathcal N_k}\pi_{k,N}K_N(x,y)\tau_N,
 \qquad
 \mu_{xy}^{(k)}=\frac{B_{xy}^{(k)}}{A_{xy}^{(k)}}.
\]
The completed-square identity in Theorem
\(\mathrm{thm{:}response\mbox{-}type\mbox{-}minimax\mbox{-}games}\)
shows that \(\mu_{xy}^{(k)}\) is the unique squared-error Bayes action on such a cell.  For a difference \(j\), the corresponding \(W\)-fiber is
\[
 \mathcal F_j=\{(x,y):x-y=j\},\qquad W=2j.
\]
If \(\mu_{xy}^{(k)}=c_j\) at every positive-mass cell in \(\mathcal F_j\), then aggregation over the fiber gives
\[
 \frac{\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal F_j}B_{xy}^{(k)}}
 {\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal F_j}A_{xy}^{(k)}}
 =
 \frac{\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal F_j}A_{xy}^{(k)}c_j}
 {\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal F_j}A_{xy}^{(k)}}
 =c_j.
\]
Thus constancy of the full-count posterior means is exactly the posterior equation required for one scalar action on that positive-mass fiber.

At \(n=2\), the hypergeometric kernel for the three support states of \(\pi_2\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
(x,y)&A_{xy}^{(2)}&B_{xy}^{(2)}&\mu_{xy}^{(2)}\\ \hline
(1,0)&\frac14+\frac12\frac12=\frac12&\frac14&\frac12\\[2pt]
(0,1)&\frac14+\frac12\frac12=\frac12&-\frac14&-\frac12 .
\end{array}
\]
These are the only positive-predictive-mass cells, and they lie in the distinct fibers \(W=2\) and \(W=-2\).  Their posterior means equal \(g_2(2)\) and \(g_2(-2)\), respectively.

At \(n=4\), put
\[
 h=\frac{\sqrt3-1}{4},
 \qquad
 z=z_4=\frac{3-\sqrt3}{2}.
\]
The two pure-effect states have prior mass \(h\), and the zero-effect state has prior mass \(z\).  The latter state assigns probabilities \(1/6,2/3,1/6\) to \((2,0),(1,1),(0,2)\), respectively.  Hence
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
(x,y)&A_{xy}^{(4)}&B_{xy}^{(4)}&\mu_{xy}^{(4)}\\ \hline
(2,0)&h+\frac z6&h&z\\[2pt]
(1,1)&\frac{2z}{3}&0&0\\[2pt]
(0,2)&h+\frac z6&-h&-z .
\end{array}
\]
For the first row, the displayed posterior identity follows from
\[
 h(1-z)=\frac{(\sqrt3-1)^2}{8}
 =\frac{2-\sqrt3}{4}
 =\frac{(3-\sqrt3)^2}{24}
 =\frac{z^2}{6},
\]
which is equivalent to \(h/(h+z/6)=z\); the third row follows by arm exchange.  The three positive cells belong to \(W=4,0,-4\), respectively, and their posterior means equal the corresponding values of \(g_4\).

At \(n=6\), cancellation of the common positive factor \(B_6\) in the seven prior weights gives the positive-difference posterior equations
\[
 \mu_{(2,0)}^{(6)}=\mu_{(3,1)}^{(6)}
 =\frac{2}{3(1+C_6)}=v_6,
\]
\[
 \mu_{(2,1)}^{(6)}
 =\frac{1/10}{3/20+9D_6/20}
 =\frac{2}{3+9D_6}=u_6,
\]
and
\[
 \mu_{(3,0)}^{(6)}
 =\frac{A_6/2+1/10}{A_6/2+3/20+D_6/20}=z_6.
\]
The first equality uses \(1+C_6=2/(3v_6)\).  The second uses
\[
 3+9D_6
 =3+\frac{2-3u_6}{u_6}
 =\frac2{u_6}.
\]
For the third, cross multiplication reduces the assertion to
\[
 10A_6(1-z_6)=3z_6+z_6D_6-2,
\]
which is precisely the defining equation for \(A_6\).  The positive-mass zero-difference cells \((1,1)\) and \((2,2)\) receive predictive mass only from zero-effect support states, so their first target moments vanish and their posterior means are zero.  Arm exchange changes \((x,y,\tau_N)\) to \((y,x,-\tau_N)\), and therefore supplies the negative-difference equations.  It follows that the posterior mean is \(z_6\) on the positive part of the \(W=6\) fiber, \(v_6\) at both \((2,0)\) and \((3,1)\) in the \(W=4\) fiber, \(u_6\) on the positive part of the \(W=2\) fiber, zero on the \(W=0\) fiber, and the corresponding negatives on the reflected fibers.  These values are exactly \(g_6(W)\).

The preceding posterior calculations fix the Bayes actions only on positive-predictive-mass cells.  The scalar rules in Definitions
\(\mathrm{def{:}n2\mbox{-}certificate}\),
\(\mathrm{def{:}n4\mbox{-}certificate}\), and
\(\mathrm{def{:}n6\mbox{-}algebraic\mbox{-}certificate}\)
also specify the prior-null cells.  The exhaustive risk calculations certified by Theorems
\(\mathrm{thm{:}n24\mbox{-}equality}\) and
\(\mathrm{thm{:}n6\mbox{-}seven\mbox{-}state\mbox{-}saddle}\)
then give
\[
 \max_{N\in\mathcal N_2}R_N^W(g_2)=\frac14,\qquad
 \max_{N\in\mathcal N_4}R_N^W(g_4)=1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\qquad
 \max_{N\in\mathcal N_6}R_N^W(g_6)=s_6^2,
\]
with every state outside the respective prior support strictly below the corresponding value.  Thus a scalar completion controls every remaining state at each of the three equality sizes, and those same two theorems yield
\[
 \rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}=\rho_n^W\qquad(n=2,4,6).
\]

At \(n=8\), both cells \((1,0)\) and \((2,1)\) lie in \(\mathcal F_1\), because
\[
 2(1-0)=2=2(2-1).
\]
Nevertheless, Definition
\(\mathrm{def{:}n8\mbox{-}full\mbox{-}upper\mbox{-}certificate}\)
gives
\[
 t_8(1,0)=\frac{73084}{10^6}
 \neq
 \frac{152579}{10^6}=t_8(2,1).
\]
Consequently \(t_8\) is not representable as \(g(W)\).  This exhibited within-fiber variation alone would not prove minimax loss.  The decisive certificate is the strict primal-dual comparison in Theorem
\(\mathrm{thm{:}n8\mbox{-}strict\mbox{-}separation}\):
\[
 \max_{N\in\mathcal N_8}R_N^{\mathrm{CR}}(t_8)
 =U_8<L_8\leq\rho_8^W.
\]
Indeed, for every scalar rule \(g\), the definition of \(\rho_8^W\) implies
\[
 \max_{N\in\mathcal N_8}R_N^W(g)
 \geq\rho_8^W
 \geq L_8
 >U_8.
\]
Hence no scalar completion can reproduce the certified full-count risk envelope.  Since the positive even sizes not exceeding eight are \(2,4,6,8\), equality at the first three sizes and strict separation at the fourth show that the second count first changes the minimax envelope at eight.  The posterior-fiber equations explain why scalar saddles close at \(2,4,6\), while the risk sandwich, rather than within-fiber variation by itself, certifies their failure at \(8\).  This argument makes no assertion for any later even size.

By the declared type of \(n\), the admissible population sizes are the positive even integers.  Consequently,
\[
 \{n\in 2\mathbb Z_{>0}:n\leq 8\}=\{2,4,6,8\}.
\]
Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}n24\mbox{-}equality}\) gives
\[
 \rho_2^{\mathrm{CR}}=\rho_2^W=\frac14
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \rho_4^{\mathrm{CR}}=\rho_4^W=1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.
\]
Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}n6\mbox{-}seven\mbox{-}state\mbox{-}saddle}\) gives
\[
 \rho_6^{\mathrm{CR}}=\rho_6^W=s_6^2.
\]
Finally, Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}n8\mbox{-}strict\mbox{-}separation}\) gives the strict inequality
\[
 \rho_8^{\mathrm{CR}}<\rho_8^W.
\]
Thus equality holds at each admissible size below eight and fails at eight.  It follows that
\[
 \{n\in 2\mathbb Z_{>0}:n\leq8,\ \rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}=\rho_n^W\}
 =\{2,4,6\}.
\]
Because \(W=2(X_1-X_0)\) is precisely the stipulated compression of the full observation \((X_1,X_0)\), the strict inequality at \(n=8\) says exactly that this compression is minimax-lossy there.  Since no other admissible positive even size lies between six and eight, \(n=8\) is the first such size.

Fix \(L_{\mathrm{bd}}<U_{\mathrm{bd}}\) and abbreviate \(\Delta=\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}=U_{\mathrm{bd}}-L_{\mathrm{bd}}>0\).  We first establish the direction in which the binary minimax result transfers to the bounded cube.  For a binary potential-outcome schedule \((Y_i(1),Y_i(0))_{i=1}^n\), define its endpoint embedding by
\[
 y_{id}=L_{\mathrm{bd}}+\Delta Y_i(d),\qquad d\in\{0,1\}.
\]
This schedule belongs to \([L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]^{2n}\), and its bounded causal average treatment effect is
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(y_{i1}-y_{i0})
 =\frac{\Delta}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\{Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\}
 =\Delta\tau_N.
\]
Given any measurable estimator \(\widehat\tau\) in the bounded problem, define the induced estimator on labeled binary observations by
\[
 \widetilde\tau\bigl(Z,(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}})_{i=1}^n\bigr)
 :=\Delta^{-1}\widehat\tau
 \bigl(Z,(L_{\mathrm{bd}}+\Delta Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}})_{i=1}^n\bigr).
\]
Division is valid because \(\Delta>0\).  Under the assignment law in \(\mathrm{ass{:}uniform\mbox{-}exact\mbox{-}balance}\), the squared-error risks obey the pointwise identity
\[
 \mathbb E_Z\!\left[
 \left\{\widehat\tau-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(y_{i1}-y_{i0})\right\}^2
 \right]
 =\Delta^2\mathbb E_Z\!\left[\{\widetilde\tau-\tau_N\}^2\right].
\]
Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}response\mbox{-}type\mbox{-}minimax\mbox{-}games}\) shows, using clipping and permutation averaging, that the minimax risk over all such labeled binary-data estimators is exactly \(\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}\).  Hence, for each \(\widehat\tau\), its supremum over the endpoint subclass is at least \(\Delta^2\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}\).  The endpoint schedules are a subclass of the bounded schedules, so taking the infimum over \(\widehat\tau\) gives
\[
 \mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{bal}}[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 \geq \Delta^2\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}. \tag{1}
\]
This argument invokes the two-count orbit reduction only on the binary endpoint subclass and makes no such reduction for nonbinary schedules.

We next compare the lower bound in \((1)\) with the independent-design affine upper bound from \(\mathrm{lem{:}hull\mbox{-}independent\mbox{-}affine\mbox{-}upper}\).  For \(n=2\), Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}n24\mbox{-}equality}\) gives \(\rho_2^{\mathrm{CR}}=1/4\).  Since \(\sqrt2>1\),
\[
 \rho_2^{\mathrm{CR}}=\frac14>\frac1{(\sqrt2+1)^2}.
\]
For \(n=4\), the same theorem gives \(\rho_4^{\mathrm{CR}}=1-\sqrt3/2\), while
\[
 1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}>\frac19
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \sqrt3<\frac{16}{9}.
\]
Both sides of the last inequality are positive, and squaring proves it because \(3=243/81<256/81\).  Since \((\sqrt4+1)^{-2}=1/9\), this is the required comparison at \(n=4\).

For \(n=6\), Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}n6\mbox{-}seven\mbox{-}state\mbox{-}saddle}\) gives \(\rho_6^{\mathrm{CR}}=s_6^2\).  Its isolating interval implies
\[
 s_6>\frac{29066256529188}{10^{14}}>\frac{29}{100}.
\]
Moreover \(\sqrt6>2449/1000\), because both sides are positive and
\[
 6>\frac{2449^2}{10^6}=\frac{5997601}{10^6}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 s_6(\sqrt6+1)>
 \frac{29}{100}\frac{3449}{1000}
 =\frac{100021}{100000}>1.
\]
All factors are positive, so squaring and dividing yields
\[
 \rho_6^{\mathrm{CR}}=s_6^2>\frac1{(\sqrt6+1)^2}.
\]
For each \(n\in\{2,4,6\}\), combining this strict inequality with \((1)\) and the conclusion
\(
 \mathfrak R_n^\star[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 \leq\Delta^2/(\sqrt n+1)^2
\)
of \(\mathrm{lem{:}hull\mbox{-}independent\mbox{-}affine\mbox{-}upper}\) proves
\[
 \mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{bal}}[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 \geq\Delta^2\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}
 >\frac{\Delta^2}{(\sqrt n+1)^2}
 \geq\mathfrak R_n^\star[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]. \tag{2}
\]

It remains to establish the sharper independent-design certificate at \(n=8\).  For integers \(k,\ell\geq0\) with \(k+\ell\leq8\), let
\[
 H_{k,\ell}:=
 \sum_{j=0}^{\ell}2^{-\ell}\binom\ell j
 \left(d_{8,k+j}-\frac{2k+\ell}{8}\right)^2.
\]
This is the normalized shifted-binomial risk appearing in \(\mathrm{lem{:}hull\mbox{-}bounded\mbox{-}global\mbox{-}reduction}\): the endpoint observation has law \(k+\operatorname{Binomial}(\ell,1/2)\), and the normalized target is \((2k+\ell)/8\).  Every coordinate of the vector in \(\mathrm{def{:}n8\mbox{-}independent\mbox{-}upper\mbox{-}certificate}\) lies between \(0\) and \(2\), so \(d_8\in[0,2]^9\) is feasible.  Set
\[
 D_0=2^{14}10^{12}=16384000000000000,
 \qquad
 \sigma_{k,\ell}=D_0(I_8-H_{k,\ell}).
\]
Direct substitution of the nine integer numerators defining \(d_8\), followed only by common-denominator arithmetic, gives the following complete list; row \(k\) lists \(\sigma_{k,0},\ldots,\sigma_{k,8-k}\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
k&(\sigma_{k,0},\ldots,\sigma_{k,8-k})\\ \hline
0&(4577441792,3880130560,30789297309696,0,238862336,
53461707285504,105693419993088,97336380346880,3580346880)\\
1&(327965806819328,359818810488832,281843022690304,293958109724672,
358362791708672,371515404700672,283644940700672,97336380346880)\\
2&(660197382158336,530887778891776,581356140759040,631689073692672,
560408945692672,371515404700672,105693419993088)\\
3&(787093695625216,855369846626304,824582262626304,631689073692672,
358362791708672,53461707285504)\\
4&(985221165627392,855369846626304,581356140759040,293958109724672,
238862336)\\
5&(787093695625216,530887778891776,281843022690304,0)\\
6&(660197382158336,359818810488832,30789297309696)\\
7&(327965806819328,3880130560)\\
8&(4577441792).
\end{array}
\]
All entries are nonnegative, and the only zeros occur at \((k,\ell)=(0,3)\) and \((5,3)\).  Since \(D_0>0\), it follows exactly that
\[
 \max_{\substack{k,\ell\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\\k+\ell\leq8}}H_{k,\ell}
 =I_8=\frac{481065022279}{8000000000000},
\]
with precisely those two maximizers.  The Bernstein-extension and separate-coordinate convexity conclusion of \(\mathrm{lem{:}hull\mbox{-}bounded\mbox{-}global\mbox{-}reduction}\) applies to this feasible endpoint action: the associated estimator is measurable under independent \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) assignment, its risk is separately convex in every normalized potential-outcome coordinate, and therefore its maximum over the bounded cube is attained at an endpoint vertex and equals the displayed maximum over \((k,\ell)\).  Thus
\[
 \mathfrak R_8^\star[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 \leq\Delta^2 I_8. \tag{3}
\]

By Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}n8\mbox{-}strict\mbox{-}separation}\), \(C_8\leq\rho_8^{\mathrm{CR}}\).  Combining this fact with \((1)\) gives
\[
 \mathfrak R_8^{\mathrm{bal}}[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 \geq\Delta^2C_8.
\]
Exact subtraction of the two rational certificate values yields
\[
 C_8-I_8
 =\frac{1489964546219114077997554988878251203581}
 {282893788917485944245799445288000000000000}>0.
\]
Because \(\Delta^2>0\), this strict rational inequality and \((3)\) prove
\[
 \mathfrak R_8^{\mathrm{bal}}[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 \geq\Delta^2C_8
 >\Delta^2I_8
 \geq\mathfrak R_8^\star[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]. \tag{4}
\]
Equations \((2)\) and \((4)\) establish the asserted strict suboptimality at exactly \(n\in\{2,4,6,8\}\).  Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}hull\mbox{-}bounded\mbox{-}minimax\mbox{-}risks}\) makes clear that \(\mathfrak R_n^\star\) optimizes jointly over all assignment laws and all measurable estimators, whereas \(\mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{bal}}\) fixes balanced complete randomization.  No step above supplies a comparison for any even \(n\geq10\), so the uniform-in-\(n\) conjecture remains open.
